section.title: Checking the examples
section.para: The world is checked automatically every time the site is built. A build with a problem stops. The checks are layered like the world itself.

section.title: The world against the UBL 2.5 model
section.para: Every document in the world is checked against the UBL 2.5 semantic model:

listitem.para: every place where a party is mentioned exists in the structure of that document type;
every mandatory party element at document level is filled;
every party of the world takes part in at least one document.

section.title: Only what UBL 2.5 endorses
section.para: The examples use only document types, associations and properties that UBL 2.5 endorses. Anything the model marks as deprecated is rejected. A transport service, for example, is invoiced with the Invoice, because the Freight Invoice is deprecated.

section.title: Nothing empty, nothing implied
section.para: Two rules of the UBL specification shape the data the world needs:

listitem.para: No empty elements (IND5). A UBL document never contains an element without content: an aggregate needs a child, a basic element a value, and a value of only spaces counts as empty. Every party element must therefore hold at least one of its parts, even though none of them is mandatory in the schema. The identity of every party makes sure there is always something to put in it.

One text per language (IND7, IND8). Two sibling text elements of the same name never have the same languageID, and never both lack one. A text element repeats only to give the same text in another language, as the bilingual notes do; several keywords of an item therefore go in one search string. The text elements are the basic properties whose data type in the UBL 2.5 model is Text or Name: their schema types derive from the CCTS text type, which carries languageID.
No empty attributes (IND9). Every attribute that is present has a value.

An absence carries no meaning (IND6). Leaving an element out never says anything; the sender states every value that matters, and every sum (section 2.2.2, "Manifest Values"). An order without a carrier does not say that the seller arranges the transport: its delivery terms must say so. The world therefore requires values that would otherwise be implied, such as the delivery terms of every order.

section.title: The parties
section.para: The identity of every party is checked: every party has a name and every organisation an identifier; tax numbers and account numbers carry valid check digits; the city in the address is the nearest town or locality of the party's own country and state; every account is held at a bank of the world in the same country; and a bank named in a document is the bank where that party keeps its account. The ISIN of a listed company has the structure and check digit of ISO 6166 and starts with its country's code.

section.title: The items
section.para: Units and packaging types must be codes of the UBL default lists; world item numbers carry a valid check digit and are unique; prices are positive and in the seller's currency; gross weight is at least net weight. Every party that bills or offers in a document has items to put on its lines, and every party with items bills or offers them. The exchange rates between the currencies agree with each other.

section.title: The map and the code lists
section.para: The map is checked as a structure: one connected road network per landmass, houses on streets, nothing built on roads or water, believable terrain, and customs posts where roads cross a border.

The world's code lists are made from one source, world/codelists/lists.json, and the committed files must be what it makes. The country and currency lists hold exactly the codes of the countries layer. No invented code may be a real one: the currencies are checked against ISO 4217 and the market identifier codes against ISO 10383, both kept in world/codelists/sources. A copy of a real list may hold only codes that its source has.

section.title: The codes in the documents
section.para: The build gives every code its list. A code must be a code of its list, compared exactly, so en is not EN; the element gets the list's listID, and its reason says what the code means in the list. A text next to a code, such as CertificateType beside CertificateTypeCode, carries the list's name for the code. The build also checks what agrees between codes:

listitem.para: every allowance and charge has a reason code;
a tax exemption reason comes from the list of the seller's country;
a payment's clearing channel is one its payment system has, and the service level fits it (decision Q18);

the packing group and the packaging danger level of a UN number agree (I and 1, II and 2, III and 3, NA and 4), the hazardous category is the class, and an emergency card belongs to a class of the goods;
a size class follows from the company's headcount and turnover.

section.title: The example documents
section.para: The build checks that a reference to another document of the same flow quotes that document's UUID wherever it gives one. Every example document is validated in the two phases UBL prescribes:

listitem.para: Phase 1: against the UBL 2.5 runtime schema of its document type, from the endorsed set.

Phase 2: its coded values against the code lists, using context/value associations (CVA). It runs twice. First UBL's own phase 2, unchanged, with the UBL default code lists. The world replaces some of those lists, so this run may object only to values in their contexts: the countries and currencies, the lower-case languages, the allowance and charge codes, and the lists to which the world gives a listID. Then the world's own associations (world/codelists/UBL-World-2.5.cva), which replace UBL's: every code element must carry the listID of its list and a code of that list. An element with several meanings is bound by its parent element; an allowance by its ChargeIndicator (UN/EDIFACT 5189 for an allowance, 7161 or 5189 for a charge); where a context allows several lists, the listID chooses. A code element that no association covers is an error, unless it is a code a party defines for itself. The attributes are checked too: currencyID against the world's currencies, unitCode and mimeCode against UBL's lists, and languageID as a BCP 47 tag, a language of the world's ISO 639 list with an optional region.

section.para: The committed examples must also be up to date: they are generated again from the world's layers and compared, so a change in the world cannot leave an example behind.

section.title: Still to come
section.para: Later layers add their own checks: document lines with items and quantities, amounts and taxes that add up, dates in a believable order, references between documents, and quantities that agree from order to invoice. These apply to the example documents as they are generated for every flow.
